//: PERMISSIONS POLICY for the GitHub Actions deploy role (rules.md R-55).
Attach to the same role as gh-actions-trust-policy.json. That file says WHO may assume the role;
this one says WHAT the role may then do.
⚠️ DO NOT PASS THIS FILE TO THE AWS CLI. It is annotated source. The `"//"` keys below are not
legal in an IAM policy document — the grammar admits only Version/Id/Statement at the top level
and Sid/Effect/Principal/NotPrincipal/Action/NotAction/Resource/NotResource/Condition inside a
statement — and AWS rejects the whole document with `MalformedPolicyDocument: Syntax errors in
policy`, naming no key and no line. Render it first, which also substitutes the placeholders:
python scripts/render_iam_policies.py --account-id <ID> --github-owner <O> --github-repo <R>
and use the output in infra/iam/rendered/. The renderer refuses on any leftover placeholder and
checks the 10,240-char inline-policy limit, so both of the late confusing failures are moved here.
NOT AdministratorAccess. R-55 forbids it, and the reason is specific rather than ceremonial: this
role is assumable by an automated system triggered by a git push. Its blast radius is whatever a
compromised or merely mistaken workflow file can reach, so the interesting question is not 'can it
deploy' but 'what is the worst a bad `run:` line can do'. With AdministratorAccess the answer is
'anything in the account'. With this policy the answer is 'deploy this project, push these three
image repositories, and stop the runtime'.
THE SHAPE IS UNUSUAL AND DELIBERATE: this policy grants almost nothing DIRECTLY.
CDK v2 does not create resources with the caller's own credentials. `cdk deploy` assumes the four
bootstrap roles (`cdk-hnb659fds-*`) that `cdk bootstrap` provisioned, and those roles do the
work — CloudFormation itself runs as `cfn-exec-role`. So statement 1 is the whole deploy grant,
and it is four `sts:AssumeRole` calls. There is no `ec2:*`, no `rds:*`, no `ecs:CreateService`
here, and their absence is not an oversight to fix the first time a deploy fails.
Consequence worth stating plainly: the privilege boundary is the CFN execution role, which IS
broadly privileged. This policy does not make a malicious workflow harmless — it makes it
auditable, because every mutation arrives through CloudFormation as a stack event with a diff,
rather than as an out-of-band API call that leaves no trace in the stack's history.
REPLACE BEFORE USE: <AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>. Region literals are already pinned (ap-south-1 for the
runtime, us-east-1 for the cost-safety plane) — that pinning is load-bearing, see statement 8.
A literal <AWS_ACCOUNT_ID> fails closed: an unparseable ARN matches nothing.
IF A DEPLOY FAILS WITH AccessDenied: add the one action the error names, scoped to the one resource
it names. Do not widen to a service wildcard, and do not attach AdministratorAccess 'temporarily' —
the temporary attachment is the one that is still there at the demo (aws-setup-instructions.md §4.3).
1. THE DEPLOY GRANT, in full.
Exactly the four roles `cdk bootstrap` creates under the default `hnb659fds` qualifier:
deploy-role           — drives CloudFormation
file-publishing-role  — uploads templates and assets to the staging bucket
image-publishing-role — pushes CDK-built container assets to the staging ECR repo
lookup-role           — read-only context lookups (this is what resolves availability-zones)
The trailing `-<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>-<region>` is spelled out per region rather than wildcarded so
that this role cannot assume a bootstrap role in a region nobody is watching. `hnb659fds` is a
constant, not a hash: it is the default qualifier and it is identical in every account. If the
account was bootstrapped with `--qualifier`, these eight ARNs are wrong and every deploy fails
with a clear AssumeRole error naming the role it wanted.
us-east-1 is here because CostSafetyStack deploys there (bin/app.ts) and needs its own bootstrap.
2. Bootstrap version check. The CDK CLI reads this parameter to decide whether the account's
bootstrap stack is new enough for the template it is about to deploy. Read-only, one parameter.
Denying it produces `SSM parameter /cdk-bootstrap/hnb659fds/version not found` — which reads as
'the account is not bootstrapped' and sends you to re-bootstrap a perfectly good account.
3. ECR login. `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken` does not support resource-level permissions — it mints
a registry-wide token, so `*` is the only scope IAM can express here, not a shortcut. The token
it returns is still constrained by statement 4: it authenticates to the registry, it does not
authorise a push.
4. Push and pull, on the three project repositories only.
`BatchGetImage` and `DescribeImages` are what let CI resolve a pushed tag back to its sha256
digest, which is the value passed to `cdk deploy --context gatewayImageDigest=` (R-51, R-56).
NOT GRANTED, on purpose:
ecr:CreateRepository  — the three repositories are Phase-0 infrastructure with immutable tags
and lifecycle policies. A workflow that can create a repository can
create a fourth one without those properties and push a mutable tag.
ecr:DeleteRepository, ecr:BatchDeleteImage — tag immutability is the promotion guarantee; a
delete grant is a way around it. Retention is the lifecycle policy's
job (keep-last-15), and that runs as ECR, not as this role.
ecr:PutImageTagMutability, ecr:PutLifecyclePolicy — same reason: a workflow must not be able
to relax the constraints the workflow is audited against.
5. stop-runtime.yml — the mutation half. This is the workflow that must run at the end of every
session without exception (rules.md R-30), so its permissions are the ones that must never be
the reason it fails.
TWO ACTIONS, NOT ONE, and the second is the one people leave out. Setting the ECS services to
desired 0 stops the tasks and leaves the `g4dn.xlarge` running and billing. Setting the ASG's
DesiredCapacity to 0 without also setting MinSize/MaxSize to 0 lets the ASG restore capacity on
its next scaling evaluation. Both grants are required for 'stop' to mean stopped; the same
reasoning is implemented in lambda/runtime-stopper/index.py.
The ASG ARN wildcards ONLY the UUID segment that AWS generates. The group NAME is exact, so this
cannot resize an unrelated auto-scaling group in the account.
6. Verification reads, and the migration task — all resource-scoped.
⚠️ THIS STATEMENT MUST NOT CONTAIN `*` IN Resource. A single `*` alongside specific ARNs does not
narrow anything: IAM evaluates the Resource list as OR, so one wildcard entry grants every action
in the statement on every resource. `ecs:RunTask` would then be account-wide, which is precisely
the grant the next paragraph claims to prevent. Actions that genuinely need `*` are in statement 6b.
`ecs:RunTask` on `gateway-migrate` only, and only in the `sih26104` cluster:
- the `:*` suffix is the task-definition REVISION, which increments on every deploy. Pinning a
revision would break the next deploy; the FAMILY is exact, so this cannot launch the Scorer
task definition, which is the one that costs money.
- the `ecs:cluster` condition is the second half. Without it, a matching task definition could
be run in any cluster in the account, including one with different security groups.
These reads are what let stop-runtime.yml PROVE it worked — print runningCount and DesiredCapacity
after the update rather than trusting that a successful API call meant a stopped instance. A stop
workflow that reports success without verifying is how a GPU bills through a weekend.
6b. The reads IAM cannot scope, isolated so the wildcard is visible and bounded.
`autoscaling:DescribeAutoScalingGroups` has no resource-level support at all — it returns groups
and filters by name in the request, not in the policy. `ecs:ListTasks` likewise takes no resource
constraint for the cluster-listing form this uses, and `ecs:DescribeTaskDefinition` has no
resource type either (a task definition is not an ARN you can scope a Describe to).
`ec2:DescribeInstances` IS THE ONE WORTH ARGUING ABOUT, so here is the argument. It is granted for
stop-runtime.yml check V-C, which sweeps the region for running `g4dn.xlarge` instances. That check
exists because V-A (ECS tasks == 0) and V-B (ASG desired == 0) are authoritative only about things
the ASG owns. An instance launched by hand during a debugging session — outside the ASG, outside
ECS — is invisible to both, and would bill at roughly $0.53/hour for as long as nobody looks.
R-30 makes stop-runtime.yml the load-bearing cost control of this entire project, so its blind
spots matter more than one extra read.
The cost of granting it, stated rather than glossed: `DescribeInstances` takes no resource
constraint, so this is account-and-region-wide visibility of instance metadata. In a single-
purpose project account that is a modest widening of a read surface that already includes ECS
services, clusters, tasks and Auto Scaling groups. It discloses topology; it changes nothing.
Kept in their own statement for one reason: a wildcard in a mixed statement is invisible, and a
wildcard in a statement containing only Describe/List actions is self-evidently read-only.
Anything added here later must be justified against that sentence. If it mutates, it does not
belong in this statement — see statement 6c, which exists because of exactly that rule.
6c. `ecs:RegisterTaskDefinition` — a mutation that IAM cannot scope, and why that is acceptable.
REQUIRED BY deploy-runtime.yml, and the reason is the digest promotion rule. `update-service
--force-new-deployment` only re-pulls whatever the existing task definition already points at, so
if that were a tag the digest inputs to the workflow would be decorative — the run would report a
digest and ship something else. The workflow therefore reads the current task definition, swaps
the container image for the digest-pinned reference, registers a new revision, and points the
service at it. That is what makes the digest the deployment unit (R-51, R-56).
`RegisterTaskDefinition` has no resource types, so `*` is the only expressible scope. The real
control on it is **statement 7**, not this one: registering a task definition is inert unless you
can also pass an execution role to it, and `iam:PassRole` here is bounded to `ComputeStack-*` and
to `ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com`. A revision registered with a role this policy cannot pass will fail
to launch. That is the security argument, and it is worth stating rather than leaving the reader
to assume a bare `*` on a mutation was an oversight.
Registering a revision outside CloudFormation DOES create stack drift on the task definition, and
that is understood and accepted: the next `cdk deploy` re-pins the family from the digest passed
as `--context gatewayImageDigest`, so the drift is corrected by the same value that caused it.
`ecs:DeregisterTaskDefinition` is deliberately NOT granted — old revisions are the audit trail of
what actually ran.
6d. CloudWatch Logs read — the R-45 execution-provider check.
GRANTED DELIBERATELY, ADDED AFTER THE FACT, and the reason is worth recording. `deploy-runtime.yml`
step V-2 tries to read the Scorer's log group to confirm it came up on `CUDAExecutionProvider`.
It was written to expect this permission to be ABSENT and to degrade to a warning naming exactly
this action and ARN — which was correct and honest behaviour against the enumerated permission set
in aws-setup-instructions.md §3.3.
But a permanent 'provider NOT verified by CI' warning is a bad equilibrium. R-45 makes a silent
CPU fallback a **failed deploy**, not a warning, because healthy-but-silently-CPU still produces
numbers — and every latency figure recorded that day is then invalid in a way nobody thinks to
check. Trading one narrow read permission for automated verification of that property is clearly
the right side of the trade.
Scoped to `/ecs/sih26104/*` and to `FilterLogEvents` only: no `DescribeLogGroups` (the workflow
names the group explicitly), no `GetLogEvents`, no write, and nothing outside the project's own
log groups. Note the trailing `:*` on the ARN — a log-group ARN in a policy needs it to match the
log streams within, and omitting it produces an AccessDenied that looks like the wrong action name.
7. iam:PassRole, scoped — the statement R-55 names explicitly.
`ecs:RunTask` requires passing the task's execution role and task role, and `iam:PassRole` is the
action that most often gets granted as `Resource: "*"`. That is a privilege-escalation primitive,
not merely untidy: with `PassRole: *` this role can hand ANY role in the account to a service it
controls the input of, and read that role's credentials out of the task it just launched. The
account's most privileged role is reachable that way.
Two independent narrowings, both required:
Resource  — `ComputeStack-*` only. CDK names roles `<StackName>-<LogicalId><Hash>`, so this
matches the Gateway/Scorer execution and task roles and nothing outside the stack.
It is a prefix wildcard because the hash is not knowable when this file is written.
Condition — `iam:PassedToService` = ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com. Even for a matching role name, it
may only be passed to ECS tasks. Passing a ComputeStack role to, say, EC2 or Lambda
is denied. This closes the gap the prefix wildcard leaves open.
7b. Invoking the RuntimeStopper directly.
The Lambda in CostSafetyStack exists to be triggered by a Budget alarm, but the same function is
also the most reliable manual stop: one call, and it performs BOTH the service stop and the
capacity stop, in the right order, with no chance of a workflow doing half the job.
us-east-1, not ap-south-1 — the function lives with the budget that triggers it and acts
cross-region on the runtime (bin/app.ts). Getting this region wrong yields a
ResourceNotFoundException on the one call an operator makes when they are already worried about
a bill.
8. The region fence, and the subtlety that makes it easy to get wrong.
An explicit Deny overrides every Allow, including any policy attached to this role later. It is
here because region drift is not a visible failure: a deploy that lands in us-west-2 succeeds,
works, bills, and is not in the region anyone opens the console to (rules.md, region discipline).
WHY GLOBAL SERVICES ARE IN NotAction. For negated conditions — StringNotEquals, StringNotLike —
an ABSENT context key makes the condition evaluate TRUE. So on any request that carries no
`aws:RequestedRegion` at all, `StringNotEquals` matches and this statement DENIES. Global service
calls are exactly the requests that may not carry it, so without this NotAction list the fence
would deny `sts:AssumeRole` — statement 1 — and nothing would deploy at all. The failure is
immediate and total, which is the good case; the bad case is a subtler one denied only sometimes.
cloudfront and budgets are listed because the CFN execution role acts on them via us-east-1 and
because both are genuinely global. us-east-1 is in the allow list regardless — that is the one
documented regional exception (cdk.json `// region`), needed for Budgets and for the Phase-4 ACM
certificate. Adding a third region here is a decision to make deliberately, not to fix a deploy.
9. Deny the credential shapes this project does not use.
The trust policy already makes this role OIDC-only, so these denies are redundant TODAY. They
are here because the failure they prevent is a quiet one: someone debugging a broken workflow
creates an access key 'just to test', it works, and the project now has a long-lived credential
that no longer appears in any workflow file. R-55 says no long-lived keys; this makes the rule
self-enforcing rather than a thing to remember.
The role-mutation denies matter more than they look. Without them this role can attach
AdministratorAccess to itself and every scope above becomes advisory — which is the specific
escalation that makes a 'least privilege' policy a decoration.
